name: Morris-Thorne Traversable Wormhole
description: A static, spherically symmetric traversable wormhole engineered to have no horizon and tolerable tidal forces. Keeping its throat open requires exotic matter that violates the energy conditions.
history: Carl Sagan had written his heroine into a black hole. In the draft of Contact, Ellie Arroway crosses the galaxy by falling into one, and Sagan, careful about such things, asked his friend Kip Thorne to check the physics before the novel went out in 1985 [sagan1985]. Thorne's answer was that a black hole kills her, its inside ending at a singularity rather than at a destination; what the story wanted was a wormhole [thorne1994]. Wormholes were not new. Einstein and Nathan Rosen had bridged two sheets of spacetime in 1935 [einstein1935], and Robert Fuller and John Wheeler had shown in 1962 that the bridge pinches off faster than light can cross it [fuller1962]. There was nothing on the shelf to hand a novelist.¶So Thorne and his graduate student Michael Morris ran the problem backwards. The usual direction is source first: write the stress-energy, solve for the geometry. They began instead from what a traveler would insist on. A throat joining two distant regions. No horizon, since a horizon is a one way door. Accelerations and tidal forces no worse than standing on the ground at home. A crossing of under a year, timed by the traveler and by those waiting at both stations. They wrote a metric meeting every item, then ran it through the Einstein tensor to see what such a geometry demands of its matter. The paper ran in the American Journal of Physics in 1988 under a subtitle that admitted its origin: a tool for teaching general relativity [morris1988].¶The demand was the surprise. At the throat the radial tension has to beat the energy density, and for a throat twenty kilometers around it runs to the pressure at the center of the most massive neutron star. Tension beating energy density means a light beam crossing the throat measures a negative energy density: the null energy condition fails, and the singularity theorems lose their footing. Morris and Thorne called the stuff exotic and declined to be embarrassed, since quantum field theory, they wrote, gives tantalizing hints that such material might be possible, and the Casimir effect makes it in a laboratory. Nor was the requirement a quirk of their ansatz. Topological censorship, proved in 1993 by John Friedman, Kristin Schleich and Donald Witt, holds that under the null energy condition any topological shortcut collapses too fast for light to cross [friedman1993]. Exotic matter is what the shortcut costs.¶The time machine nobody ordered showed up within months. Put one mouth on a ship, run it out at speed, bring it home. It has aged less than the mouth that stayed, the tunnel keeps its ends in step as seen from inside, and a walk through the throat is a walk into your own past. Morris, Thorne and Ulvi Yurtsever published that the same year, and the arguing began [morris1988prl]. Fernando Echeverria, Gunnar Klinkhammer and Thorne threw billiard balls in so that each came back out to knock its younger self off course, and found in 1991 that the grandfather paradox fails in the direction nobody expected: not too few consistent histories but too many [echeverria1991]. Sung-Won Kim and Thorne found the quantum stress-energy diverging as the machine switches on, but so feebly that quantum gravity takes over first, they argued, and the wormhole carries on regardless [kim1991]. Stephen Hawking held that the divergence wins, and answered in 1992 with chronology protection, his experimental evidence being that we have not been overrun by tourists from the future [hawking1992]. They never agreed on what counts as close to a horizon, which is really a question about quantum gravity. A novelist asked for a shortcut and got a research program.
